origin.title: Origin & Motivation
paragraphs: The idea for this website existed years ago. But back then, I always felt there was no rush, it was too early, I could wait a little longer...
But over the past year, I've felt more and more clearly: in this era of uncertainty, impermanence often strikes without notice or reason.

Seemingly healthy middle-aged peers falling ill and passing away is becoming more frequent. Single, childless, DINK, divorced, and solitary family structures are becoming normalized. Anxiety and confusion about the meaning of life spread across social media platforms. And at home, my parents on both sides, approaching eighty, are aging day by day...
These realities make it harder and harder to tell myself: 'This can wait.'

intention.title: Intention
paragraphs: I created this website not because I've already deciphered life and death and want to serve you some chicken soup for the soul...
On the contrary, it's because I've realized time and again: most of us have almost zero preparation for impermanence.

We make detailed long-term plans for education, career, family, and assets, but rarely answer a more fundamental question: 'If my life cannot continue as planned, have I reserved space to deal with impermanence?'
In reality, what truly breaks people is not 'impermanence of life and death' itself, but when it happens — no forethought, no arrangements, no consensus, no choice.

This website is less 'about death' and more 'an instruction manual on how to seriously review this life.' It cares about: how to honestly face yourself, how to systematically organize a lifetime, how to reserve some choice for yourself while accepting impermanence. So you can live earnestly, clearly, with dignity, and with joy.

preparedness.title: Readiness Check
paragraphs: This is not a test — it helps you identify your current level of preparedness. You can adjust the score at any time, just record where you are right now.
If you find it hard to judge, that's okay too — go with your intuition and give a rough range.

framework.title: Framework
paragraphs: This website is divided into two major parts and four chapters. In this era of changing family structures — single, unmarried, childless — we can no longer assume someone will always clean up our mess.

That's why building a 'life and end-of-life' preparation system for yourself in advance is not pessimism, but maturity. I sincerely hope this website can become a quiet space for you — not rushing you, not scaring you, just accompanying you to slowly organize this life clearly.

usage.title: How to Use
paragraphs: This website has four chapters. In each chapter, we guide you to use the tools and templates provided to engage in deep thinking and organization around your real life situation.

To make it easier to understand and use, the website provides demonstration examples and designs exercises as handbook tables or optional choices, reducing the burden of extensive writing and tool comprehension.

But a serious note: 'No matter how much assistance we provide, the real thinking and organizing can only be done by you.' These exercises are not about 'completing tasks' — they are about taking your life seriously, one step at a time.

reminders.title: Five Reminders
paragraphs: If you experience prolonged discomfort or emotional distress while using this website, please prioritize taking care of yourself and consider seeking professional support.

ai-knowledge-base.title: AI Knowledge Base
paragraphs: This knowledge base focuses on AI-powered Q&A about human aging, illness, death, physical and mental health, and end-of-life care. It integrates legal, medical, religious, and familial perspectives — combining serious policy interpretation with warm family experience. When facing aging, illness, or end-of-life care, you can quickly find practical information, emotional resonance, and actionable solutions.

stop-and-look.title: Stop and See Yourself
paragraphs: At some point in life, we suddenly realize: we've come a long way, yet rarely stopped to truly see ourselves.
We've been pushed forward, defined by expectations, responsibilities, and roles. Who are we? What do we want? These questions seem increasingly blurry.
This chapter invites you to pause and rediscover yourself. Not to change anything, but to see — to see the overlooked parts, to see your authentic self.

personality-tests.title: Personality Self-Assessment
paragraphs: Before diving deeper, we've prepared two classic personality assessment tools for you.

These tests can help you understand your personality traits, behavioral patterns, and thinking preferences from different angles. They're not about labeling you, but providing a reference framework for better self-understanding.
You can try one or both — there are no right or wrong answers, only deeper self-awareness.

career-values.title: Career Values Assessment
paragraphs: In career choices, what truly matters to you? Is it financial reward, a sense of achievement, or work-life balance?
Career values are the core driver of your professional decisions. Through this assessment, you'll discover your top 14 career value orientations and ultimately lock in your 3 core values.
This exercise isn't about putting a career type label on you — it's helping you clarify what you really want in your work.

ability-assessment.title: Social Ability Self-Assessment
paragraphs: Beyond personality traits and value orientations, your ability structure is another important dimension of self-understanding.

Based on McKinsey's social ability system, this assessment covers 42 core competencies across three dimensions — cognition, interpersonal, and self-management — giving you a comprehensive scan of your ability landscape.
You'll discover your strengths, potential areas, and areas for improvement — which is far more actionable than simply knowing 'I'm an INTJ' or 'I'm high in openness.'

social-roles.title: My Social Roles
paragraphs: From birth, we've been assigned various roles: child, student, employee, parent, partner...
These roles shape us, but also limit us to some extent. We've grown accustomed to defining ourselves by our roles, forgetting that beyond them, there is still an 'I.'
This exercise helps you sort through the various roles you carry and see how much space they occupy in your life.

summary.title: Rediscover Yourself
paragraphs: Through the exercises in this chapter, you may have gained new insights about yourself. These insights may be incomplete or not entirely accurate, but they are a beginning.
Self-discovery is an ongoing process, not something completed in one go. Be patient, stay curious.
questions: Through these exercises, try to identify your innate habits and temperament patterns.
What areas or abilities are you clearly superior in compared to others?
Which social role makes you feel the most tired? Why?
Which label do you most want to shed?
If you had to describe yourself stripped of all roles in one word, what would it be?
How would you like to redefine yourself?

life-countdown.title: See the Timeline of Life
paragraphs: Before discussing how to 'live positively,' we must first face a truth: time is limited.
Most people have a vague sense of 'someday' about life, never truly calculating — after sleep, work, and chores — how much truly 'self-directed' time remains.

This exercise transforms abstract lifespan into concrete visual marks. When you see the past squares already colored in and the future ones still blank, the urgency of 'living for yourself' becomes real.

emotional-check.title: Emotional State Check
paragraphs: Before discussing 'being positive,' we also need an objective understanding of our current state. Emotional shadows or chronic tension can silently dim the light in life.
We've prepared a three-dimensional assessment covering emotions, stress, and tension to help you identify potential psychological risks from a professional perspective.
This isn't about diagnosing illness, but about gaining clear awareness of your mental foundation before making active choices.

passive-vs-active.title: Chosen Life vs Active Choice
paragraphs: Looking back at your life — how many choices did you truly make yourself? How many were driven by circumstances, others, or society?
A passively chosen life is like a pre-written script; you're just an actor, an NPC following the script set by societal norms.
An actively chosen life may be full of uncertainty, but at least it is YOUR life.
Having seen the finiteness of time, think again: which life do you want?

life-fun.title: Life's Joys & Health Foundation
paragraphs: Positive living requires both the enthusiasm to experience and the physical and mental capacity to do so. Health isn't everything in life, but it is the foundation of all possibilities.

Modern psychological research (Mark Travers, 2025) shows that specific types of hobbies effectively build psychological resilience against depression and anxiety. We categorize hobbies into three types, corresponding to three layers of health protection:
'Physical Foundation' — physical hobbies (running, swimming, tai chi) maintain bodily function through physiological mechanisms, providing a physical base for mental health.
'Creative Capacity' — creative hobbies (writing, painting, cooking) provide a sense of achievement through producing tangible work, effectively combating depression and loneliness.

'Cognitive Reserve' — intellectual hobbies (reading, chess, learning new skills) continuously challenge cognitive boundaries, strengthen neural connections, and directly reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

Interest also has levels: from passive sensory stimulation ('sensory interest') to active exploration ('conscious interest') to deep alignment with personal values ('vocational interest') — the higher the level of interest, the stronger its protective power for health. High-level interests are the best brain health supplements.

health-body.title: Caring for Your Body · Investing in the Future
paragraphs: Many people equate 'living positively' with a positive mindset, forgetting that the body is the foundation that carries everything.

Alzheimer's disease is the seventh leading cause of death globally, with one new case every three seconds. However, a 2024 Lancet study shows that addressing 14 modifiable risk factors can reduce the risk by 45%.
You don't need to become a health expert. But if you want your future self to have enough cognitive and physical capacity to experience life — now is the best time to start taking action.

community-aging.title: Plan Ahead · New Community Aging
paragraphs: In previous sections, we discussed how to actively care for your body, cultivate hobbies, and manage emotions — all investments in your future. But there's a question often avoided: when there are no children by your side, who will accompany you in old age?

'No children by your side' doesn't only apply to single or childfree individuals. Children living abroad, losing an only child, estranged parent-child relationships, or children with insufficient care capacity — these situations are more common than we think. China now has over 120 million one-person households; living alone is no longer a fringe phenomenon. The traditional elderly care system assumes children as the primary caregivers, but this premise no longer holds for a growing number of people.

'New Community Aging' starts from this premise: beyond family and market-based solutions, actively building and cultivating a 'non-blood-related mutual support community.' It doesn't require you to move in with anyone right now, but asks you to start nurturing relationships that can age together with you. Meanwhile, embodied AI robots are approaching — handling monitoring, reminders, alerts, and other repetitive care tasks, allowing human energy to focus on emotional support and shared decision-making.
Placing this in the 'Live Positively' chapter is intentional: its essence is proactively arranging for your later years — just like investing in body, brain, and relationships.

summary.title: Live in the Now, Invest in the Future
paragraphs: Living positively doesn't mean trying so hard — it means living actively and with awareness.
Take care of your body and emotions. Spend time with people and things that give you meaning.
Start today, start with every small choice — for present joy and future freedom.
questions: After seeing your life countdown, what is the one thing you most want to do immediately?
How many choices in your life have you truly made for yourself?
What things in life bring you joy?
Starting today, what proactive health choices are you willing to make?
If your future self had enough mental and physical capacity, what would you most like to do?

responsibility.title: What is Responsibility
paragraphs: Everyone has responsibilities: to family, to work, to society, to oneself.
Some responsibilities we take on voluntarily; others are assigned to us. Regardless, responsibility is an indispensable part of life.
Stating clearly means facing these responsibilities honestly, not avoiding them.

responsibility-list.title: My Responsibility Checklist
paragraphs: Let's sort through your responsibilities.
Caring for family, commitments at work, promises to friends, promises to yourself...
This exercise helps you list your responsibility checklist and think about how to better fulfill these responsibilities.

three-questions.title: Three Questions for Major Decisions
paragraphs: While sorting through responsibilities, we often encounter difficult decisions: Should I accept a high-risk treatment? Should I change my current family structure? Should I hold onto a certain belief?
These decisions often affect the quality of the rest of your life. We need a more rational tool than 'going with your gut' to guide our thinking.

'The Three Questions' uses values, psychological expectations, and scarcity as three dimensions to probe deeply. It doesn't provide answers, but it acts as a mirror reflecting your truest trade-offs and boundaries, helping you make decisions without regret.

choice-rights.title: Advance Directives
paragraphs: An advance directive (Living Will) is a medical wish statement written in advance while you are still clear-minded. It's not a will giving up treatment, but a legal document that speaks for you when you can no longer make decisions.
In your final days, do you want life-sustaining medical measures? Where do you want to spend your remaining time? What things do you want your family to know that you've never been able to say?

Thoughtfully consider and articulate your five wishes — preserving your final dignity and choices. This directive isn't cold legal language; it's your final act of gentleness to your family — letting them not have to guess your wishes in difficult times.

insight-people.title: Insight into People
paragraphs: Your advance directives are written; you know clearly what you want to communicate. But next comes a more critical question: who do you entrust these matters to?

Choosing a designated agent can't rely on momentary feelings. Someone who feels reliable today may not be three years from now. True judgment comes from long-term observation — do they follow through on promises, hold up under pressure, choose wisely in conflicts of interest, and genuinely understand your values. Each fragment alone isn't enough to conclude, but accumulated over time, they form a clear picture.

The tool below helps you capture daily observations. Don't rush to conclusions — record first, accumulate first. When you're ready to make the final choice, these records will become the most weighty evidence for your designated agent assessment.

arrangement.title: Choosing Your Designated Agent
paragraphs: The observations you recorded in "Insight into People" now converge into one decision: who do you entrust these matters to? Who is the person you trust most? When you can no longer make decisions for yourself, who do you want to speak on your behalf?
A designated decision-maker isn't predetermined by birth — it's your active choice. This person could be your spouse, child, close friend, or even a professional institution.

Choosing a designated agent isn't just about picking someone 'reliable.' Consider: Do they understand your values? Can they make decisions under pressure? Are they willing to take on this responsibility?
It's time to make this judgment. Bring the observations you've accumulated in "Insight into People," and use this tool for a systematic assessment.

summary.title: Leaving No Regrets Behind
paragraphs: You've made it here, completing the core work of the 'State Clearly' chapter.

You've sorted your responsibility checklist, identified what's urgent and important, and what needs advance transition planning. You've examined the real trade-offs behind major decisions, and written down your five wishes in advance directives — those things you want your family to know but never found the words to say.

You've evaluated who can be your designated agent, and where no suitable person exists, learned about professional alternatives. These aren't cold procedures — they are your final order and tenderness left for this world.

Stating clearly isn't pessimism — it's responsibility. It ensures you leave no regrets behind. These arrangements don't need to be completed all at once — you can come back anytime to revise, supplement, or update. Life changes, and your arrangements can change too.
questions: In your responsibility checklist, which item worries you most? Have you thought of a transition plan?
Which major decision did the Three Questions help clarify the real sticking point of?
Among your five wishes in advance directives, which one do you most want your family to know?
Have you confirmed your designated agent? If not, which alternative plan will you start with?
If today were your last chance to review these arrangements clearly, how ready would you say you are?

face-goodbye.title: Facing Farewell
paragraphs: Farewell is a theme everyone must face. But we rarely talk about it proactively, rarely prepare for it.
Perhaps out of fear, perhaps out of taboo. But regardless, farewell will eventually come.
Rather than facing it passively, it's better to prepare actively. So when it arrives, you can be more composed.

no-regrets.title: Leave No Regrets
paragraphs: Before diving into the specifics of saying goodbye, let's pause for a crucial 'life rehearsal.'

If today were the end of your life, looking back — do you have unfinished dreams, unspoken words, unreconciled relationships? This isn't fear-mongering; it's a question rooted in the real regrets of hundreds of dying people.

Australian nurse Bronnie Ware recorded the top five regrets of the dying, and Fudan University research revealed the top three regrets of Chinese elderly. These cross-cultural findings point to the same truth: too many people only realize at the end of their lives — that they've been living by the wrong priorities all along.

This tool helps you assess your current life state across seven dimensions — including self-authenticity, relationship quality, health foundation — generates your 'Life Coherence Index,' and provides personalized improvement suggestions. The best farewell begins with the best way of living.

goodbye-list.title: My Farewell Checklist
paragraphs: Before saying goodbye, what things do you want to accomplish?
Some are practical arrangements; others are emotional farewells. Both are important.
This exercise helps you list your farewell checklist.

goodbye-way.title: Ways to Say Goodbye
paragraphs: Everyone has different preferences for how to say goodbye. Some want a lively celebration of life; others prefer a quiet departure. Some want the solemnity of traditional rituals; others want the freedom of a living funeral.
This tool helps you design your own farewell — from ceremony format to resting place, from farewell words to background music. Leave the world one final creative brief, your way.
There's no right or wrong — only your choice. Write these arrangements down in advance so the people you care about know your wishes.

ready.title: Final Preparations
paragraphs: Having completed the exercises above, you'll find: farewell isn't as frightening as it seems.
You simply exist in a different form. Your memories, your love, your influence continue on.
Being ready isn't about waiting for death — it's about being prepared to say goodbye.

summary.title: A Graceful Farewell
paragraphs: You've made it here, completing all the work of the 'Farewell Gracefully' chapter.

Through the Life Coherence Assessment, you've seen your true state across three dimensions — health, relationships, and self-actualization — and received your personalized improvement roadmap. You've written your farewell checklist — things you want to do before leaving. Some may already be done; others are still in progress.

You've designed your own way of saying goodbye: chosen your preferred ceremony, your ideal resting place, a farewell message for the world, and even selected background music and who to see you off. These arrangements aren't cold checklists — they are your final, gentle creative brief to the world.

Farewell is part of life, as natural as birth. Preparing in advance isn't pessimism — it's wisdom. It lets you leave without regret, without fear, without attachment. These arrangements can be revised anytime — life changes, and your farewell can change too.
May you say goodbye gracefully.
questions: In the Life Coherence Assessment, what was your index score? Which dimension was weakest? What's your first step for improvement?
How many items are on your farewell checklist? Which one are you most looking forward to completing?
In designing your farewell, which choice are you most satisfied with? Was any option surprising even to yourself?
If your farewell message were engraved somewhere, what would you want passersby to think when they see it?
If today were your last time reviewing these arrangements, how ready would you say you are? What's missing?

faces.title: As a Consultant
faces.text: Nearly 20 years, 125+ corporate clients, thousands of individual clients. I've seen the harshest side of the workplace and the most beautiful transformations. If you're at a career crossroads, I might help you see the way.

faces.title: As an HR Executive
faces.text: Since 2016, I've been the #1 HR at listed foreign companies, private enterprises, and startups. Interviewed tens of thousands, laid off thousands, and personally orchestrated organizational transformation, talent strategy, cultural重塑, and efficiency improvement. JV, MNC, private, startup — I've immersed in every organizational ecosystem. These experiences help me understand both organizational logic and individual struggles.

faces.title: As a Practicing Lay Buddhist
faces.text: Seek truth through illusions is not about escaping the mundane, but living authentically within each role. Precepts are not bondage but freedom — work is my dojo, relationships are my mirror, cultivating a clear mind amid worldly affairs.

faces.title: As a Vegetarian Lifestyle Advocate
faces.text: 13 years vegetarian — not restraint, but choice. The body is a vessel for practice; every meal is reverence for life. I believe how you treat food reflects how you treat yourself.

faces.title: As a Content Creator
faces.text: Not just writing articles — themed videos, music works, audio podcasts. Each creative form is another practice of truth. Output is not the goal; shared cultivation is.

faces.title: As a Tech Practitioner
faces.text: I vibe code, deploy AI applications, and do deep data analysis. Technology is not the end — serving human growth is. I believe the best consultant will be the one armed with AI.

faces.title: As a Project Management Expert
faces.text: PMP certified, managing every consulting project with PM thinking. From diagnosis to delivery — not just an idea, but a traceable path.

faces.title: As a Life Care Volunteer
faces.text: Life care is not charity — it's seeing. Through health education and hospice volunteering, I deeply understand the wisdom of 'prevention before illness.' The deepest compassion is teaching people to live well before illness arrives. Giving brings you closer to freedom than taking — this is the deepest lesson I've learned.

faces.title: As a Bilingual National Tour Guide
faces.text: A bilingual tour guide license — not a career backup, but opening the world through another language. Every tour is a cross-cultural shared practice.

faces.title: As a Licensed High School Chinese Teacher
faces.text: A high school Chinese teaching credential — not a career alternative, but a deep affection for my mother tongue and reverence for classical studies. Language is the foundation of culture; teaching is the best form of learning, and classics are forever the best teachers.

faces.title: Still Exploring
faces.text: 'I' is just an illusory construct, growing as sentient beings need me to master new skills. More slashes may be unlocked ahead — not because of lack, but because the world is vast and worth staying curious. Exploration itself is the answer.

coreIdeology.title: Minimal Material
coreIdeology.desc: Not ascetic restraint, but active choice. 13 years vegetarian, simple living — subtract excess desire to hear your true voice. Less in matter, more in life.

coreIdeology.title: Maximal Capability
coreIdeology.desc: 20 years across 6 industries, from trainer to Group HRD, from client-side to consultant, from HRD to Vibe Coding — always learning, always practicing. Capability is the only asset that will never betray you.

coreIdeology.title: Supreme Spirit
coreIdeology.desc: Seek truth through illusions, live toward death. Work is your dojo, relationships are your mirror, every role is practice. Supreme spirit is not transcending the mundane — it's living authentically within it.

stages.title: See Yourself
stages.desc: The starting point of all change is seeing. Seeing your patterns, beliefs, blind spots. Not judgment, but awareness.

stages.title: Personalize
stages.desc: No one-size-fits-all method. Adapt to context, tailor to the person — let every solution grow in the client's own soil.

stages.title: Live Actively
stages.desc: Not perfection in every area, but holding the foundation of work and family. Turn physical, intellectual, and creative interests into daily practice — exercise the body, feed the mind, express the soul.

stages.title: Awaken
stages.desc: Wake up from NPC to player — no longer passively executing a script, but seeing the game rules and reclaiming choice. Work is not about climbing, but refining the heart through events. Life, aging, illness, death — not fear, but inevitable stages.

methodologies.title: Context-Based Thinking
methodologies.desc: Four decision questions: Whose problem is this? What situation are they in? What is their core need? What solution can grow in this context?
methodologies.desc2: Bodhisattvas fear causes, ordinary people fear results — true masters focus on causes, not outcomes. Instead of worrying about layoffs, ask: what causes can I plant today?
methodologies.example: Facing layoffs: don't start with compensation — ask — what life stage is this person in? What do they fear most? What transition path works best for them?

methodologies.title: Practice Truth Through Roles
methodologies.desc: Cultivate your true inner self through every temporarily played role. Work is the dojo,烦恼 is bodhi — how to observe your mind's fluctuations through each arising frustration, that is the real practice.
methodologies.example: 5000+ layoff experiences: every difficult conversation is an opportunity to cultivate compassion. The layoff is 'illusion'; the empathy cultivated is 'truth'.

methodologies.title: Organizational Quadrant
methodologies.desc: Efficiency × Culture: two dimensions, four quadrants — high efficiency/high culture (thriving), high efficiency/low culture (mechanical), low efficiency/high culture (coasting), low efficiency/low culture (zombie).
methodologies.example: A mid-to-high-end hotel cluster: efficiency met target but culture was fractured → repair cultural bonds first, then restructure, avoiding hard landing.

methodologies.title: Soul Questions
methodologies.desc: What is your true inner vision? What kind of person do you want to become? How satisfied are you with yourself right now? If you had one year left, how would you live? Step deeper to reach your authentic self.
methodologies.example: A 40-year-old executive broke down when asked 'if you had one year left' — he had been living for others' expectations, never asking what he truly wanted.

quotes.text: Work is not asceticism, but it can be a dojo.
Layoffs are an organization's metabolism, but every person metabolized deserves to be seen.
True freedom is not doing whatever you want — it's still being yourself in every role you must play.
Wealth is a lesson, not an answer. What you cultivate is your relationship with desire.
Practice through every role is not escaping the mundane — it's finding the path to truth within it.
There is no one-size-fits-all method, only context-based wisdom.
Management's greatest arrogance is judging others' problems from your own situation.
Consulting is not giving answers — it's helping others grow their own.
Adapting to context doesn't mean no principles — it's principles expressed flexibly in specific situations.
Every organization's illness is known only to its own body.
Awakening is not leaving the world — it's no longer getting lost within it.
Precepts are not bondage — they draw a safe boundary for freedom.
The body is the vessel of practice. Mistreat it and you lose the right to practice.
Life's organization is not about throwing away — it's seeing clearly what's worth keeping.
Living toward death is not pessimism — it's the ultimate clarity.

services.storyP1: 5000 is not a cold number. It's 5000 late-night calls, 5000 difficult conversations, 5000 turning points in people's lives. Behind every number is a specific face, a family, a life going through its storm.
services.storyP2: At its core, working for a company is a win-win balance between organization and individual — you contribute ability and time, the company provides platform and return. But when business pivots, strategy shifts, or your own value proposition changes, this balance breaks. Whether you jump or are pushed, it's the same: balance is lost, time to choose again.
services.storyP3: I've seen a post-95 employee win the excellence award in the afternoon and get laid off that evening — not because she wasn't good enough, but because the business line was cut. I've seen an 18-year veteran HR draft her own departure agreement and sit in her car for two hours. I've also seen middle-aged people who felt relieved after being laid off: 'I've wanted to leave for a long time, I just never had the courage.'
services.storyP4: What I can do is not choose between 'cold' and 'warm' — because this work is inherently contradictory. What I strive for is: let those leaving leave with dignity, let those staying not live in fear, so that every time the balance breaks, both sides can turn around gracefully.
services.storyQuote: Layoffs are an organization's metabolism, but every person metabolized deserves to be seen.
